messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Nadia Haddad, a 63-year-old auditor who had spent most of her adult life priding herself on steadiness and precision, traced the start of her difficulties to the day her younger sister died on a hiking trip in a state park. Nadia had not been with her when it happened, but she was the one who arrived after the search team had located her. She remembered being led through scrub and dry grass to a narrow ranger outbuilding where her sister’s belongings had been placed, the door shut behind her while an officer spoke in a low voice. What fixed itself in her mind was the combination of confinement and exposure: the locked room, the smell of dirt and sun-warmed brush still clinging to the clothes, and the unbearable fact of her sister reduced to personal effects and descriptions. Ever since, natural settings that resemble that park, enclosed rooms she cannot easily leave, and anything that brings to mind victims have carried an immediate charge for her.

In the months afterward, those moments did not simply upset her; they seemed to strip away the present. If she was in a conference room with the door closed during an audit meeting, or if a client site was on the edge of wooded property, or if she saw a news story showing a grieving family and a victim’s photograph, the memory arrived all at once, without warning. She did not experience it as “remembering” in any ordinary sense. She was back there with the dry air in her throat, the stale indoor smell, the officer’s voice, and the same terror flooding her body as if the loss were happening again. She had come to believe that her body had become an enemy in this way, launching into danger signals even when she knew, rationally, that she was in an office or at home. That belief made the suddenness of these episodes feel even more ominous to her, and once she started scanning constantly for anything that might set them off, she seemed to notice more of them.

Her work gave these fears a daily stage. As an auditor, Nadia was expected to travel to unfamiliar offices, inspect back rooms, and sit through long meetings in windowless spaces with people she did not know. She now avoided unfamiliar places whenever she could, telling colleagues she preferred remote document review or asking for cases closer to home where she could control the environment. She was certain that if she entered a place she had not already mapped out, she would not be able to judge the danger quickly enough. When she could not avoid going, she stayed on guard from the moment she arrived—tracking exits, noting whether doors locked, glancing repeatedly toward hallways, and remaining keyed up through the entire visit. That watchfulness followed her into the night. Sleep became fragmented, not because of a single recurring dream she described, but because her body would not settle; she lay in bed listening for sounds and waking abruptly, already tense.

Over time, her understanding of what had happened to her hardened into darker conclusions. What frightened her most was not only that her sister had died, but that nothing she did—showing up, asking questions, trying to be composed—had changed anything. She had come to believe she could not stop bad things from happening, and from there it did not feel far to deciding that people, life, even God had proved unreliable. Those beliefs fed directly into the way she lived now. If the world was fundamentally unsafe and she was helpless in it, then staying hyperalert made sense; avoiding unknown places felt less like a symptom than common sense. But living in that state also kept proving to her that she was damaged and unprotected. Each sleepless night, each day spent braced in meetings, seemed to confirm that her body would keep reacting as though danger were present and that she could no longer trust herself to feel safe.

The same beliefs also shaped the way reminders struck her. Seeing a victim’s memorial on the local news or even passing a roadside display of flowers could hit with unusual force because it seemed to place her sister among all the other people the world had failed to protect. On weekends, when friends suggested a botanical garden or an outdoor fundraiser, Nadia often refused before she had fully thought it through; natural surroundings had become charged in her mind, not only with memory but with the conviction that terrible things can happen anywhere and no one can prevent them. The more she lived this way—avoiding, scanning, sleeping poorly—the more easily the full sensory reliving broke through, and each episode left her feeling more helpless and more estranged from the faith and trust she once relied on.

She finally sought help after leaving a client meeting in embarrassment when the conference room door clicked shut and she felt the entire scene rush back so vividly that she could barely breathe or orient herself. She told the therapist she was afraid she was “losing the ability to be in the world,” afraid that her work would narrow until she could no longer do it, and afraid that every reminder of another person’s suffering would keep dragging her back to her sister’s death. What she hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget her sister, but to be able to enter a room, sleep through the night, and walk past reminders of loss without feeling that terror take over her whole body again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Nadia’s negative beliefs directly lead to or intensify the intrusive trauma memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly show, within one paragraph, that Nadia’s sense of threat causes or strengthens her negative appraisals or beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that Nadia’s ongoing sense of threat makes triggers/reminders more likely to be noticed or activated.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time, her understanding of what had happened to her hardened into darker conclusions. What frightened her most was not only that her sister had died, but that nothing she did—showing up, asking questions, trying to be composed—had changed anything.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once she had come to see herself as helpless in the face of disaster, the memory itself grew more punishing and easier to trigger; when it broke through, she was not only back in that ranger outbuilding, but back there as the person who could do nothing, which made the scene feel even more immediate and inescapable.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When she could not avoid going, she stayed on guard from the moment she arrived—tracking exits, noting whether doors locked, glancing repeatedly toward hallways, and remaining keyed up through the entire visit. That watchfulness followed her into the night.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling this endangered so often gradually became, in her own mind, evidence that something fundamental had changed in her—that she could no longer rely on the world, or even on herself, to feel basically safe.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She had come to believe that her body had become an enemy in this way, launching into danger signals even when she knew, rationally, that she was in an office or at home. That belief made the suddenness of these episodes feel even more ominous to her, and once she started scanning constantly for anything that might set them off, she seemed to notice more of them.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living at that level of alarm made the world feel crowded with warnings: a closed door, a patch of dry brush outside a client site, even a brief image of a bereaved family on television could register almost instantly as a cue that something was wrong.
<<<END>>>
